806.title: Written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:30–33)
806.hook: a new covenant: "in their heart will I write it"
806.carry: a line no exile can carry off
806.howItsDone: Jews read this promise as part of Jeremiah's chapters of comfort; learning blessings and verses such as the Shema by heart is a familiar part of Jewish education.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rachel wept for her children, and her tears were called work that would be rewarded: there is hope. Today, in the same chapter, a promise about where God's teaching will live.

Torah gets written on a lot of surfaces. On tablets of stone, carried down a mountain. On parchment, rolled into a scroll and lifted in the synagogue. On a tiny scroll tucked into a case on a doorpost, because Deuteronomy says to write these words upon the posts of thy house. Ink, stone, wood. Every one of them can be lost, broken, or left behind when you're carried into exile. In the middle of his chapters of comfort, Jeremiah names one more surface, one that goes wherever you go.
screen: `STONE, PARCHMENT, DOORPOST.` → `ALL CAN BE LEFT BEHIND.` → `ONE MORE SURFACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the promise. "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." Not like the covenant made with their ancestors on the day God took them by the hand out of Egypt, which they broke. And then: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." My law: in Hebrew, torati, my Torah, my teaching. The text doesn't promise a new set of words. It's the same teaching, in a new place. Not outside you, on stone, where you have to go and read it, but inside, simply part of who you are. Deuteronomy already reaches for this: these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart. Proverbs says it too: write them upon the table of thine heart. Jeremiah's twist is who does the writing. In his promise, God writes. And the next verse draws out what that would mean: no one will need to teach a neighbor, "for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest." Some Jewish readers hear this as the hope of a day when Torah is so deeply learned that it's second nature, like a language you grew up speaking. There's a small version within reach of anyone: a line learned by heart is a line no exile can carry off.
screen: `A NEW COVENANT.` · then, large: `IN THEIR HEARTS WILL I WRITE IT.` · then: `THE SAME TEACHING, A NEW PLACE.` · `FROM THE LEAST TO THE GREATEST.`

segments.voice: Choose one line from these days on Jeremiah's road, it was never about your size, or there is hope, or today's: I will write it in their hearts. Say it slowly, once, under your breath, then close your eyes and say it again without looking. Say it once more on the out-breath, and let it be yours.
Torati. Hebrew for "my teaching": Jeremiah's promise of a covenant where it is no longer only on stone or parchment, but inside. Today's word.
Your line: a line no exile can carry off. The same teaching, in a new place. Day eight hundred six, done.

807.title: Buy the field (Jeremiah 32)
807.hook: as Jerusalem falls, Jeremiah buys a field as a sign that people will return
807.carry: plant the tree, sign the lease
807.howItsDone: Jews read Jeremiah 32:6–27 as the haftarah for the Torah portion Behar, which sets out the law of redeeming family land, and the purchase at Anathoth is often taught as a picture of acting on hope during disaster.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new covenant, not on stone this time, but a line no exile can carry off. Today, a promise gets written into a deed and sealed in a jar.
screen: `A LINE NO EXILE CAN CARRY OFF.`

segments.voice: The army of Babylon is camped around Jerusalem. Jeremiah is locked in the court of the prison, because the king doesn't like what he keeps saying: that the city will fall. Then his cousin Hanamel shows up with a business offer. He has a field back home in Anathoth, the family land, and by the law of the family, Jeremiah has the right to redeem it. Buy my field, he says. The land is about to be in enemy hands. The seller knows it. The buyer is in jail. And Jeremiah says yes.
screen: `BABYLON AROUND THE WALLS.` → `THE PROPHET IN PRISON.` → `A COUSIN SELLING A FIELD.`

segments.voice: Jeremiah does the whole deal properly. He weighs out the silver, seventeen shekels, the text says. He signs the deed, seals it, calls witnesses. There are two copies, one sealed and one left open. He hands them to his scribe, Baruch, in front of everyone in the prison court, and tells him to put both in an earthen jar, so they will last a long time. Why the fuss? Because this isn't really a purchase. It's a sign. In the King James words: "Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land." People will buy and sell here again. Life will come back. And here is the human part. Right after the deal, Jeremiah prays, and admits that the siege mounds are already at the walls. He did the right thing, and he still seems unsure. The answer comes back as a question: "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?" Then the promise is repeated, almost word for word: fields shall be bought in this land. Notice the order. The hope isn't a feeling first and an action after. Jeremiah pays first, while the city is still under siege. A hope that costs something, gets written down, and gets sealed in a jar for later. Some readers take it as a picture of a hopeful act when nothing around it looks hopeful: plant the tree, sign the lease, put the deed in the jar.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that seems unlikely right now, a friendship that cooled, a plan you shelved, something in your life that looks besieged, and ask what one small down payment on it would look like: a message, a seed in a pot, a date on the calendar. Let one answer come, and hold it the way Jeremiah held the deed before he handed it to Baruch. If you pray, you can bring that hope before God.
Anathoth, Jeremiah's family land, which he bought from prison as a sign that Babylon's siege wouldn't be the end. Today's word.
Your line: plant the tree, sign the lease. Jeremiah paid before he felt sure. Tomorrow, a scroll meets the fire.

808.title: Write it again (Jeremiah 36)
808.hook: the king burns the scroll column by column, and Jeremiah dictates it again
808.carry: there were added besides unto them many like words
808.howItsDone: Jews read Jeremiah 36 among the Latter Prophets, and the scene of Baruch writing at Jeremiah's dictation is often taught alongside the care Jewish tradition gives to handwritten scrolls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah paid silver for a field in a city about to fall: plant the tree, sign the lease. Today, the words themselves go into the fire.

A penknife. A brazier of coals. A long roll of writing. It's winter, and King Jehoiakim sits in his winter house with a fire burning on the hearth in front of him. A man named Jehudi is reading aloud to him from a scroll: every warning Jeremiah has spoken, written down by the scribe Baruch. Every time Jehudi finishes three or four columns, the king cuts that piece off with the penknife and drops it into the fire. He listens to the whole thing, piece by piece, until the entire scroll is ash.
screen: `A WINTER HOUSE, A FIRE.` → `THREE OR FOUR COLUMNS AT A TIME.` → `THE WHOLE SCROLL IS ASH.`

segments.voice: Jeremiah is barred from going to the Temple, so he dictates his words, and Baruch writes them in a roll. Baruch reads it aloud in the Lord's house, on a fast day. Some officials hear it and are shaken. They tell Baruch: go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are. Then they tell the king, and he sends for the scroll. The king and his servants who heard all these words were not afraid, and did not tear their garments. But a few officials, Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah, begged the king not to burn the scroll. He would not listen. So the fire wins. Or seems to. Then comes a short instruction, in the King James words: "Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll." Jeremiah dictates, and Baruch writes, all over again. And the chapter ends with a quiet detail: there were added besides unto them many like words. The second scroll is longer than the first. That's what this chapter seems to hand down: a king can burn a page, but he can't burn the person who remembers it, or the friend holding the pen. Jewish custom treats a worn-out Torah scroll with care, burying it rather than throwing it away, and new scrolls are written by hand, letter by letter. The answer to the knife and the fire is a scribe, a fresh roll, and patience.
screen: `BARUCH READS IN THE TEMPLE.` · `SOME BEG THE KING TO STOP.` · then, large: `TAKE THEE AGAIN ANOTHER ROLL.` · then: `THE SECOND SCROLL IS LONGER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that slipped away, a recipe from someone who's gone, a story your grandfather told, a plan that burned down, and gather what you can, one piece at a time, the way Jeremiah spoke and Baruch wrote. Don't worry about getting it exact; if something new arrives that wasn't in the first version, let it in too. If you pray, you can ask for help remembering.

809.title: By the river Chebar (Ezekiel 1)
809.hook: among exiles in Babylon, a vision of a chariot of fire and wheels
809.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 1 as the opening of the book of Ezekiel, and in many communities it is chanted as the prophetic reading on the first day of Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king burned Jeremiah's scroll, and the prophet and Baruch wrote it all again, with more. Today, a new prophet, far from home.
screen: `THERE WERE ADDED BESIDES UNTO THEM MANY LIKE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Where does God live? For many in Judah, the answer had an address: Jerusalem, the Temple, the holy of holies. Now some of them have been carried off to Babylon. They sit by the river Chebar, a long way from that address. Among them is Ezekiel, whom the text calls a priest, far from the Temple where priests serve. And his book opens there, in the King James words: "as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God." Not in Jerusalem. In exile.
screen: `GOD HAD AN ADDRESS.` → `CAPTIVES BY THE RIVER CHEBAR.` → `THE HEAVENS WERE OPENED.`

segments.voice: What Ezekiel sees is hard to describe, and he knows it. A whirlwind comes out of the north, a great cloud, fire folding in on itself, a glow like bright metal at the center. Out of it come four living creatures, each with four faces: a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. They have wings, and they move straight ahead without turning. Beside them are wheels, as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel, their rims full of eyes. Wherever the spirit goes, the wheels go too. Above is a firmament like crystal, then a throne, and on it a figure like a man, surrounded by brightness like a rainbow in the clouds. Listen to how careful the language is. Ezekiel almost never says this is what it was. He says the appearance of, the likeness of, as it were. At the top, he piles them up: "This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD." Three layers of distance before the name of God. Jewish tradition calls this vision the merkavah, the chariot. The Mishnah treats it with great caution: it is not to be taught even to one student, unless he is wise and already understands on his own. Mystics later built a whole path of contemplation around it. But the plain meaning is enough for today. The throne has wheels. The glory that seemed tied to one building shows up beside a river in a foreign land, right there with the exiles.
screen: `A STORM, FOUR LIVING CREATURES.` · `A WHEEL IN THE MIDDLE OF A WHEEL.` · then, large: `THE APPEARANCE OF THE LIKENESS OF THE GLORY.` · then: `THE THRONE HAS WHEELS.`

segments.voice: If you can, go to a window or step outside, and find something in motion: a cloud, a bird, branches, even a ceiling fan. Just watch it move, without naming or explaining it; Ezekiel was standing in an ordinary place, by a river in a foreign land, when the sky opened. If you pray, you can pray from right where you are, the way the exiles had to.

810.title: Eat this scroll (Ezekiel 3:1–3)
810.hook: the prophet eats a scroll and it is "as honey for sweetness"
810.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 2–3 as the prophet's call, and some communities mark a child's first lesson in Hebrew letters with honey so that learning tastes sweet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by the river Chebar, the heavens opened and Ezekiel saw the merkavah: God in exile too. Today, the vision gives him something to eat.

"Open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee." That's what Ezekiel hears, right after the vision. A hand reaches toward him, holding a scroll. It's unrolled before him, and it's written on both sides, front and back. And the text tells us what's written there: lamentations, and mourning, and woe. A scroll of bad news, inside and out. Not a scroll to read aloud, or file away, or hand to someone else. He is told to eat it.
screen: `A HAND HOLDING A SCROLL.` → `WRITTEN FRONT AND BACK.` → `LAMENTATIONS, MOURNING, WOE.`

segments.voice: Here is how the text tells it, in the King James words: "Son of man, cause thy belly to eat, and fill thy bowels with this roll that I give thee. Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." Stop on that. The words on the scroll are grief. The taste is honey. The message hasn't changed; it's still lamentation and woe, and the rest of his book will be full of hard news. What changes is that it's no longer outside him. He's swallowed it, and the word of God, even when it's heavy, tastes sweet in his mouth. Notice the order too. Before he speaks a single word to the exiles, he takes the words in. Only then is he told: go, get thee unto the house of Israel, and speak with my words unto them. The book of Psalms has a line close to this: the judgments of the Lord are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. And Jewish life has a custom that makes the picture real. In some communities, on a child's first day of learning Hebrew letters, honey is put on the letters, or on a slate, and the child licks it off. Learning should taste sweet. The scroll Ezekiel eats isn't a children's lesson. It's hard. But the image holds both: words you take all the way in, even difficult ones, can become part of you, and that can be sweet.
screen: `OPEN THY MOUTH, AND EAT.` · then, large: `AS HONEY FOR SWEETNESS.` · then: `TAKE THE WORDS IN FIRST.` · `HONEY ON THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Pick one line you've read recently, from scripture, a book, a letter, or use Ezekiel's: it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness. If you pray, you can let that line become your prayer for now.

811.title: The watchman (Ezekiel 33:1–9)
811.hook: a watchman must warn, whether or not anyone listens
811.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 33 among the Latter Prophets; the duty to warn and to act when someone is in danger is also taught from the Torah's command not to stand idly by a neighbor's blood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezekiel ate a scroll of mourning and woe, and it was sweet as honey. Today, he is given a job title.

Who is supposed to say something? A smoke alarm chirping in the apartment next door. A friend about to drive home after too many drinks. A coworker about to send an email to the wrong list. Each is the same moment: knowing something the other person doesn't, and wondering whose place it is to speak. Ezekiel 33 opens with exactly that question, set on a city wall. A city chooses one of its people and sets him up high to watch the road. When he sees danger coming, he blows the trumpet.
screen: `WHO IS SUPPOSED TO SAY SOMETHING?` → `A MAN ON THE CITY WALL.` → `SEE DANGER, BLOW THE TRUMPET.`

segments.voice: The chapter lays it out like a case of law, two ways. First case: the watchman sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet. Someone hears it and ignores it, and the sword takes him; his blood is on his own head. The watchman did his part. Second case: the watchman sees the sword coming and stays quiet. Then the responsibility falls on the watchman. Then God turns the picture toward Ezekiel himself, in the King James words: "So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me." And if you warn, and the person does not turn, "thou hast delivered thy soul." The watchman is responsible for seeing and for speaking, not for what people do with the warning. That can be a relief. It also takes away every excuse for silence. And the warning isn't meant as a threat. A few verses later comes the reason for all of it: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live." The point of the trumpet is not to be right. The point is that people live. Jewish ethics has its own form of this. The Torah says, do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbor, and the rabbis read it as a duty to act when someone is in danger. A watchman isn't a scold. He's someone who cares enough to make a sound.

segments.voice: Ask yourself whether there's a warning you've been sitting on: someone running too hard, a risk a friend can't see, a tire that looks low. Find the one sentence and, in your mind, say it kindly, without blame, the way you'd want to hear it. Notice that after you say it, the choice is theirs; if you pray, you can bring that person before God.
The watchman. Set on the wall to see danger and blow the trumpet; Ezekiel is told he is the watchman for his people. Today's word.
Your line: the watchman warns. What they do with the warning is up to them. Until tomorrow.

812.title: Shepherds who feed themselves (Ezekiel 34)
812.hook: leaders who fleece the flock; God will seek the lost and bind the broken
812.howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 34 among the Latter Prophets, and the image of the leader as shepherd is taught through the stories of Moses and David caring for their flocks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the watchman on the wall: see the danger, blow the trumpet, and leave the choice to them.

Ezekiel has been speaking to exiles who have lost almost everything: their land, their Temple, their king. Today he turns from the people to the people in charge. In his chapter, the leaders of Israel are called shepherds, an old picture for anyone whose job is to feed and keep a flock. And he has a question for them, the kind that stings because the answer is obvious.
screen: `EXILES WHO LOST EVERYTHING.` → `NOW, THE PEOPLE IN CHARGE.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE SHEPHERDS.`

segments.voice: The question is blunt. In the King James words: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?" Then the charges, one by one. You eat the fat and wear the wool. You kill the well-fed ones. But the weak you have not strengthened. The sick you have not healed. The broken you have not bound up. The ones driven away you have not brought back. The lost you have not looked for. Instead, you ruled them with force and with harshness. So the sheep scattered, became food for wild animals, and no one went looking for them. It isn't a list of grand crimes. It's neglect: a leader who takes what the job gives and skips what the job asks. Then the chapter turns, and God says, in effect: then I will do it myself. "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick." Almost every failure on the first list is answered by a promise on the second. The text even judges between sheep and sheep: the strong ones who push with shoulder and horn and muddy the water the others have to drink. The Bible says that Moses and David both kept sheep before they led anyone. A midrash tells that Moses was chosen after he followed one runaway young goat to a pool of water and carried it back on his shoulders. The leader in this chapter goes looking for the one who wandered off.
screen: `SHOULD NOT THE SHEPHERDS FEED THE FLOCK?` · `THE WEAK, THE SICK, THE BROKEN, THE LOST.` · then, large: `I WILL SEEK THAT WHICH WAS LOST.` · then: `MOSES AND THE RUNAWAY GOAT.`

segments.voice: Think of a flock that's yours already: a kid, a team, a younger sibling, an aging parent, a friend who leans on you. Go down Ezekiel's list slowly, who's weak, who's sick, who's been hurt, who has drifted away, and let one face come. Just hold that person, the way a shepherd might carry a stray back; if you pray, you can pray for them by name.
